title: The US-India Trade Deal Is '99% Done.' Here's What's Left — and What's at Stake.
excerpt: US Ambassador Sergio Gor says only the last one per cent remains, but behind the optimism lies a fraught final stretch over agriculture, tariffs, and the political will to close.
body:
When Sergio Gor, the US Ambassador to India, took the stage at the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum Leadership Summit in Washington on Tuesday, he did something diplomats rarely do: he put a number on it.

"We are in the final steps on this deal. Most of this deal is complete. There are a few items that remain on both sides. It's in the last one per cent of that deal," Gor told a room of business leaders and policymakers from both countries.

After eighteen months of back-and-forth — framework agreements, high-level summits, and a trade relationship shadowed by tariffs and trust deficits — the US-India bilateral trade agreement is, by Gor's account, nearly done.

## What Brought Us Here

The contours of the deal were first sketched out on February 7, 2025, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump issued a joint statement outlining the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement. India agreed, in principle, to lower tariffs on industrial goods and several agricultural products. In return, Washington offered a preferential 18 per cent tariff — significantly lower than the rates facing competing Asian exporters like Vietnam and Bangladesh.

At the time, the calculus seemed straightforward: with Trump's sweeping IEEPA tariffs adding a punishing 50 per cent surcharge on many countries, the deal gave India a competitive edge.

Then the US Supreme Court struck down those global tariffs. Overnight, the leverage shifted. Indian negotiators found themselves weighing whether the concessions they had offered still made strategic sense without the threat of a tariff wall.

"There is less appetite now for tariff concessions that could spike imports without delivering equivalent export gains," a senior Indian government source told The Hindu Business Line last week.

## The Last One Per Cent

The remaining sticking points are not trivial. Agriculture remains the most politically charged. American trade negotiators want greater market access for US farm products — dairy, poultry, and genetically modified crops — while Indian policymakers face intense domestic pressure from farm organisations warning that cheap imports could devastate local farmers.

India is also seeking assurances on the legal mechanism Washington will use to give it a tariff advantage over competitors. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, speaking in London last week, was blunt: "The day that happens, the deal is on."

The US Trade Representative's ongoing Section 301 probe — alleging overcapacity and forced labour practices across 60 economies including India — has added another layer of friction, even as negotiators at the working level push to close.

## The Bigger Picture

Despite the complications, the diplomatic temperature is warm. Gor cited the personal equation between Trump and Modi as a driving force, noting that the President "still talks about" his visit to India with great fondness and is looking forward to returning.

The ambassador also revealed that Quad foreign ministers will convene in the Philippines in approximately two weeks — on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting — signalling that the broader US-India strategic relationship continues to deepen in parallel with trade talks.

The proposed deal, if sealed, would provide the regulatory certainty that businesses on both sides have been asking for, particularly in sectors like technology, pharmaceuticals, and clean energy where bilateral trade has been growing rapidly. Bilateral trade between the two countries reached approximately $200 billion in fiscal year 2025-26.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora in the US, the trade deal carries direct implications. A stable bilateral trade framework could smooth the path for Indian tech professionals navigating an uncertain visa landscape, create new business corridors for NRI entrepreneurs, and signal the kind of durable partnership that transcends election cycles.

But the clock is ticking. With US midterm elections in November and political attention increasingly consumed by domestic issues, the window for closing may be narrower than the "99 per cent done" framing suggests. As one trade analyst put it: "In trade negotiations, the last one per cent is always the hardest — and the most expensive."

*Sources: The Hindu Business Line, Outlook Business, IANS, Reuters, Devdiscourse*
